Arrow is good if you enjoy the soap opera style drama.

Seriously, if you like Spiderman or the X-men and you just said "that ain't me" you need to have a long look in the mirror right about now.

posts.name: Reckless
posts.cooked:
phantaskippy:

Seriously, if you like Spiderman or the X-men and you just said “that ain’t me” you need to have a long look in the mirror right about now.

At least Peter Parker acts like he cares about the people in his life (Amazing Spider-Man being an exception). Everyone is so hateful, passive-aggressive, and relentlessly inconsiderate on Arrow. And the fight scenes are quite impressive for a live action costumed hero show. Are they the best in the costumed/super hero genre? Not even close. But that aspect of it is much, much stronger than the melodrama.

I don’t dislike the show, but the part of it I dislike is the same as many of DC’s other live-action endeavors: There is no levity. Tony Stark cracks jokes. Steve Rogers fumbles around a pretty girl. Thor trades quips with his best frenemy brother. But Arrow and Man of Steel? There is very little fun to be had.

posts.name: Edwin
posts.cooked:
Reckless:

I don't dislike the show, but the part of it I dislike is the same as many of DC's other live-action endeavors: There is no levity. Tony Stark cracks jokes. Steve Rogers fumbles around a pretty girl. Thor trades quips with his best frenemy brother. But Arrow and Man of Steel? There is very little fun to be had.

At least if you go back to Smallville, you get a certain lightness…not much in the way of humor, but a lot of somewhat charming character interaction and not just constant grimness.  I think that the campiness of the old Batman and Superman TV shows and humors has left DC in general a little gun-shy about trying to make their characters funny.  Which, of course, they shouldn't; real humor almost never arises from effort in that direction, but rather from talent and spontaneity that some people just don't have.  When people who aren't funny get told by the network that they have to write comedy, bad things happen; the networks have never managed to figure this out.

posts.name: jagarciao
posts.cooked: The studios haven't either. If you look at the progression of funny, quirky, witty, but still badass characters in movies you see that once the studios realize what it is about a character and start trying to write to those traits they start to fail. Look at Tony Stark... from first movie to third movie his character almost becomes a caricature of himself. Subtlety and nuance brought in by an actor putting his spin on a part was hindered by the fact that writers started to try to throw in those subtleties and nuances into the part. Same thing happened with Johnny Depp's Captain Jack Sparrow.
